extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy and literature (general public interested in Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for admitting, judging, or composing poetry in a well-ordered State — focused on whether poetry is truthful, educative, and consistent with reason rather than appealing to irrational passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of imitative poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: To the rejection of imitative poetry, which certainly ought not to be received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitative poets (tragedians, epic poets) are 'imitators' thrice removed from the truth and therefore ruinous to the understanding of hearers; their art imitates appearances rather than realities and so is unfit for admission into a well-ordered State. The text repeatedly argues for excluding such poetry because it nourishes the inferior parts of the soul and impairs reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must aim at realities (not mere appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitator creates appearances only; the painter paints appearances, not the true form—the imitator is far removed from truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art that only reproduces appearances (like a painted bed) lacks access to the form/idea and therefore cannot convey truth. When judging or producing poetry/art, prefer works that strive toward realities or truth, not mere deceptive likenesses that please by appearance alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poets should have genuine knowledge of the subjects they depict
rubrics_metrics.description: We have a right to ask poets about subjects they treat (military tactics, politics, education) to see whether they truly know them; imitators may speak well in metre yet lack real knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poets on whether they possess practical knowledge (e.g., legislation, military skill, arts) underlying their depiction. Evidence such as having educated followers, having effected reforms, or having practical accomplishments supports their claim to be instructive rather than mere imitators (example: contrast Homer with legislators like Solon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must be useful to the State and to human life (not merely delightful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let poetry's defenders show not only that she is pleasant but also useful to States and to human life, and we will listen kindly; but if there is no use, the art may be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or admitting poetry, require demonstration of civic or moral utility. Pleasure alone is insufficient; poetic works should be shown to contribute to the education, order, or virtue of the polis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit only hymns to gods and praises of famous men
rubrics_metrics.description: Hymns to the gods and praises of famous men are the only poetry which ought to be admitted into our State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a strict content standard for a 'well-ordered State', permit poetic forms that honor the gods or celebrate exemplary figures; exclude lyric/epic/tragedy that dwell on passions or imitation unless they can be demonstrated to serve reason and virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poetry that strengthens the irrational or passionate parts of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry feeds and waters the passions (pity, lust, anger) instead of drying them up; it lets the irrational nature rule, impairing reason and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poems for their psychological/moral effects: if a work encourages excessive pity, weeping, lust, anger, or other ungoverned passions, it is harmful. Prefer works that foster self-control, measure, and obedience to law and reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not praise or admire in others what one would condemn in oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: We delight in pity at another's misfortune when recited by poets, but in private we value patience and would condemn such behavior; thus praising others' unmanly lamentations is unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral inconsistency induced by poetry: if a poem invites admiration for conduct that citizens would find shameful in themselves, it is pernicious and should be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience susceptibility — popular poetry appeals to passions not reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative poet who aims at being popular prefers the passionate and fitful temper, which is easily imitated by the ignorant multitude; such poetry does not address the rational principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When admitting or programming poetry (e.g., at public festivals), consider the audience's tendency to imitate and be moved by spectacle; avoid works that manipulate crowds' emotions and thereby undermine civic reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge artists by whether their work produces educative and practical followers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man could educate and improve mankind, he would have many followers and be honored; genuine teachers (e.g., Pythagoras) leave a way of life and disciples—poets who lack this record are likely mere imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical/biographical criteria: look for evidence that a poet's teaching had a lasting, practical educational effect (schools, disciples, legislative influence) rather than mere admiration for artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer testimony of the knowledgeable user over that of the mere imitator
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three arts: one which uses, another which makes, a third which imitates. The user (practitioner) knows the right form and indicates goodness; the imitator lacks this knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating representations of technical activities (e.g., cobbling, flute-making), give weight to the judgments of practitioners and users rather than scenic depictions by poets/painters who imitate without understanding.
